title: Stored biological samples enable highly sensitive personal information disclosure
description: Sending a physical sample into long-term freezer storage creates a repository of biological material from which sensitive health, genetic, or biometric information may later be derived beyond the immediate storage purpose. The privacy risk is located at the Physical Sample Storage because retention of the specimen preserves a rich source of personal data for future access, testing, or secondary use.
assumptions: The physical sample remains linkable, directly or indirectly, to a data subject or study record, and stored samples may be accessible for later analysis.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selection is best-effort because PANOPTIC is primary here and the exact LINDDUN threat-tree mapping for biological sample storage is approximate.

title: Retained biological samples create an attractive target for unauthorized access or misuse
description: By placing the physical sample into freezer storage, the datastore accumulates sensitive biological specimens whose compromise could expose intimate information about data subjects. The threat is not merely generic security loss: the existence of stored biospecimens increases the risk of privacy data breach involving genetic, health, or identity-revealing material.
assumptions: The storage facility may be accessed by multiple personnel or systems, and samples are valuable for analysis or identification.
uncertainty_note: This is grounded in the privacy sensitivity of biological sample collection/storage; PANOPTIC match is strong for PA03.11, but the exact LINDDUN breach node is approximate.

title: Stored biospecimens may enable linkability across studies or records
description: Once the wet lab deposits the sample into physical storage, the specimen can serve as a stable identifier or quasi-identifier that allows correlation across study batches, repositories, or later analyses. Even if direct identifiers are removed, the sample and its associated metadata may permit linking the same person across contexts.
assumptions: Sample labels, freezer locations, chain-of-custody records, or intrinsic properties of the specimen can be correlated with other records.
uncertainty_note: Linkability is a plausible PANOPTIC-aligned threat for biological sample handling, but it depends heavily on labeling and repository practices not stated in the flow description.

title: De-identified sample ID may still enable re-identification in the wet lab
description: The flow sends a 'de-identified ID' from LIMS to the Wet Lab for use on the sample. If the identifier is only pseudonymized, deterministic, or otherwise linkable to other records available to the Wet Lab or adjacent systems, the sample metadata may remain identifiable or become re-identifiable. This creates a risk that the wet lab can associate the sample back to a person despite the intended de-identification.
assumptions: Assumes the Wet Lab or connected operational context may have access to auxiliary information, prior labels, or stable mappings that could link the returned ID to an individual.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC match PA06.07 is strong because the flow explicitly concerns de-identification quality, but the exact re-identification feasibility depends on how the ID is generated and what other data the Wet Lab can access.

title: LIMS may issue an insufficiently de-identified identifier for downstream sample handling
description: At the point of generating and transmitting the sample identifier, LIMS may fail to apply adequate de-identification or minimization. If the identifier embeds meaning, remains stable across contexts, or is reversible without strong separation controls, downstream use in the Wet Lab may exceed the privacy protection expected for de-identified sample handling.
assumptions: Assumes the identifier is created or assigned by LIMS and that de-identification quality is a privacy requirement for this workflow.
uncertainty_note: Using LINDDUN type Nc here is a best-effort mapping from PANOPTIC PA06.07, which is associated with both Dd and Nc; the threat is framed as insufficient policy/control over de-identification rather than direct disclosure alone.

title: Stored raw sequence data enables broad disclosure of sensitive genomic information
description: The flow transfers digital raw sequence data into long-term storage. Raw genomic sequence data is itself a rich digital artifact that can reveal sensitive traits, disease predispositions, ancestry, and potentially information about relatives if accessed or later used beyond the original storage purpose. Persisting this artifact in the cluster filesystem increases the privacy impact of any unauthorized or excessive access.
assumptions: Sequence data is linked or linkable to a person or sample provenance within the surrounding system, or remains inherently sensitive due to its identifying and inferential nature.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 'Recording' is an approximate but reasonable PANOPTIC grounding here because the flow stores a digital artifact; PANOPTIC may also have a more storage/disclosure-specific activity not present in the retrieved context.

title: Raw sequence data may be insufficiently de-identified before storage
description: If the sequence data is stored with direct identifiers, stable sample IDs, or remains inherently identifiable due to uniqueness of genomic data, the dataset may not be de-identified enough to protect the data subject. Storing such data in the filesystem creates risk of personal data disclosure even when explicit identifiers are removed.
assumptions: The stored sequence data concerns human subjects or otherwise personal biological samples, and de-identification or pseudonymization is expected before or during storage.
uncertainty_note: This applies only if de-identification is intended or required in the system context; raw genomic data can remain identifiable even after removal of obvious identifiers.

title: Stored sequence data can support re-identification or identity inference
description: Once raw sequence data is placed in the cluster filesystem, it can be matched with reference datasets, metadata, or prior pseudonymous records to re-associate the data with a specific individual. Even if initially separated from identity attributes, the stored genomic content may later enable re-identification or strong identity inference.
assumptions: Attackers or internal users may have access to auxiliary datasets, metadata, or sample linkage information enabling matching.
uncertainty_note: PA05.01.01 is clearly relevant if the data has been de-identified or pseudonymized; if the data is already directly identified, this is more identity inference than re-identification.

title: Single-source profiling from raw sequence data during compute preparation
description: As raw digital sequence data is transferred from the cluster filesystem to compute nodes for transformation, the compute environment can assemble and organize subject-level genomic or sequence-derived attributes from that single source. Even before objective-specific transformation completes, sequence data can enable correlation of variants, markers, or other subject-linked characteristics, creating a profiling risk.
assumptions: Assumes the sequence data is personal data or can reasonably be linked to identifiable data subjects, as is often true for genomic or human-derived sequence datasets.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC retrieval favored profiling activities, which plausibly apply here because raw sequence data is highly information-rich. The exact PANOPTIC sub-activity may differ if the primary risk is instead downstream analysis rather than organization/profile construction at transfer/ingest time.

title: Targeting of specific data subjects based on transformed or inferable sequence attributes
description: Once compute nodes receive raw sequence data, they can distinguish particular data subjects or categories of subjects for different treatment based on inferred traits, biomarkers, ancestry, disease associations, or other sensitive characteristics. This creates a risk that the processing pipeline supports subject targeting beyond the original objective.
assumptions: Assumes compute-side processing can derive or use subject-level distinctions from the sequence data and that those distinctions could influence decisions, access, prioritization, or subsequent actions.
uncertainty_note: This is a plausible downstream-use threat grounded in PANOPTIC's Targeting activity, but the flow description itself only states transformation into objective-specific data; it does not explicitly confirm discriminatory or treatment-selection logic.

title: Delivered research data may be made available beyond its permitted lifecycle or audience
description: This flow copies context-relevant research data from the cluster filesystem into the data delivery DMZ specifically to make it available for delivery. That availability step can create a disclosure threat if the dataset remains exposed in the DMZ longer than necessary, is retained after the legitimate delivery purpose ends, or is reachable by broader recipients than intended. In PANOPTIC terms, this aligns with Affording revelations: making protected information available at the conclusion of its lifecycle or outside the intended protection boundary.
assumptions: Assumes the DMZ is a staging area for external or semi-external delivery and may have broader accessibility or weaker retention controls than the source filesystem.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selection is best-effort because PANOPTIC was requested instead of strict LINDDUN DFD-position analysis; PA10.01 fit is strong, but the exact Dd subtree may vary by catalog version.

title: Transferred dataset may exceed the approved scope for delivery
description: The flow moves generated research data into a delivery zone. If the transferred contents include fields, records, or categories not covered by the delivery purpose, sharing agreement, or consent basis, the action leverages data outside established limits. This is a privacy threat because the DMZ becomes a point where out-of-scope data is staged and potentially disclosed.
assumptions: Assumes there are contractual, ethical, consent, or policy limits on what subset of research data may be delivered.
uncertainty_note: PA06.08 appears applicable when the delivery package can contain extra attributes or records, but the flow description does not explicitly confirm over-broad content.

title: Request for physical sample may disclose sensitive biological material beyond what is necessary
description: The flow requests release of a physical biological sample from the DNA Store to support sequencing. A biological sample can reveal highly sensitive health and genetic information about the data subject, so requesting or releasing the sample for downstream use creates a privacy threat if more specimen material or richer specimen access is provided than is necessary for the stated research purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the stored sample is linked or linkable to an identifiable person and that the request can trigger release or preparation of the specimen for shipment.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC PA03.11 is a close fit because the flow concerns handling a biological sample, although the action here is a request/retrieval from storage rather than initial collection from the data subject.

title: Sample request can enable re-identification of pseudonymized specimen records
description: To fulfill the physical sample request, the DNA Store may need to map a research request to a particular stored specimen and associated donor identity or code. If the sample inventory was previously de-identified or pseudonymized, this lookup and release step can re-associate the specimen with the individual, enabling re-identification.
assumptions: Assumes the DNA Store maintains a key, metadata, or operational process that can reconnect specimen identifiers to a specific data subject.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on whether specimen records are in fact de-identified/pseudonymized before request handling.

title: Sample release request may violate regulatory or consent restrictions
description: The DNA Store's handling of the request may deviate from regulatory, ethics, or consent requirements if the requested physical sample is released for sequencing without a valid legal basis, required approvals, or alignment with the donor's consent and governance constraints.
assumptions: Assumes the sample is subject to human-subjects research, biobank, HIPAA/GDPR, or consent-governed restrictions on secondary use and transfer.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine risk for biobank/sample-transfer flows, but the exact governing rule set is not provided in the prompt.

title: Researcher obtains an identifiable biological specimen beyond what is necessary
description: When the NCCoE Researcher retrieves the physical sample from the DNA Store, they gain direct access to a biological specimen that can inherently reveal sensitive personal information (e.g., genetic identity, health traits, familial links). If the sample is retrieved in excessive quantity, with unnecessary identifiers, or for a broader purpose than the request authorizes, this creates a disclosure risk through over-collection/access to the specimen itself.
assumptions: Assumes the physical sample is linkable to an identifiable or reasonably re-identifiable data subject and that access controls or minimization constraints may be insufficient at retrieval time.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC match PA03.11 is not a perfect fit because the flow is retrieval from storage rather than initial collection from the data subject, but it is the closest retrieved sub-activity involving direct handling of a biological specimen.

title: Retrieval of the physical sample enables linkage of specimen to the requesting context or individual
description: By retrieving the physical sample referenced by the request, the NCCoE Researcher may be able to link the specimen to a particular participant, case, or request context. Even if the sample is not explicitly named in the flow description, accompanying labels, storage metadata, or chain-of-custody context can make the specimen linkable to a specific data subject.
assumptions: Assumes sample containers, request references, or storage procedures include identifiers, pseudonyms, or contextual metadata that permit linkage.
uncertainty_note: Linkability depends on how specimens are labeled and whether the researcher can access associated metadata; the PANOPTIC citation is approximate.

title: Research subject may be unaware that their biological sample is being physically retrieved for this use
description: The act of retrieving a stored biological specimen for researcher use may occur without the data subject's knowledge at that moment, especially where samples are retained and reused over time. This can make the subsequent use of the specimen insufficiently detectable to the individual, particularly if no notice, audit visibility, or participant-facing trace of retrieval exists.
assumptions: Assumes the participant does not have real-time visibility into each reuse or retrieval event involving their stored sample.
uncertainty_note: Detectability is inferred from the reuse of stored specimens; the flow itself does not prove absence of notice or audit transparency.

title: Sample retrieval may pre-empt the data subject's ability to object or change privacy choices
description: If the NCCoE Researcher retrieves the physical sample before the data subject can exercise updated preferences, withdraw participation, or narrow permitted uses, the retrieval action can effectively bypass the person's control over that use of the specimen.
assumptions: Assumes there is a mechanism or expectation for withdrawal, objection, or updated privacy settings, but retrieval can occur before those preferences are applied to the specimen request workflow.
uncertainty_note: PA07.09 is conceptually relevant if withdrawal/manageability timing exists, but the flow description alone does not confirm such a control path.

title: Collection of a biological sample creates a direct identifiability risk
description: Receiving the physical sample constitutes collection/handling of biological material. A biological specimen can itself be inherently identifying or readily linkable to a specific individual, especially if accompanied by shipment metadata or labels, creating a detectability/identifiability privacy threat at the sequencing lab intake point.
assumptions: Assumes the physical sample is derived from or associated with a human data subject and is not irreversibly anonymized before transfer.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort mapping: PANOPTIC PA03.11 clearly fits the biological sample transfer, while the exact LINDDUN tree node is approximate because PANOPTIC is being used instead of strict DFD-position threat trees.

title: Recording and accessioning the sample may expose the subject's presence in the dataset
description: When the receiving clerk records, labels, or accession-tracks the incoming sample, a physical artifact and associated intake record are created that represent the subject. This can make the subject's participation or presence in the research pipeline discoverable beyond what is necessary.
assumptions: Assumes normal lab intake includes logging, labeling, or otherwise recording receipt of the sample.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 Recording is inferred from standard receiving-clerk workflow rather than explicitly stated in the flow description.

title: Sample collection/receipt could exceed the authorized research scope
description: This transfer may result in the sequencing lab receiving a biological sample whose collection or downstream use exceeds the bounds set by consent, protocol, ethics approval, or other governing rules. The privacy threat arises if the sample is accepted despite being out of scope for the stated research purpose.
assumptions: Assumes there are scope limits from consent, IRB/protocol, contract, or policy that govern what samples may be received and processed.
uncertainty_note: The out-of-scope issue is a conditional threat: it applies when intake controls do not verify that receipt of the sample is within the permitted collection/processing scope.

title: Patient may be asked to provide a biological sample without sufficient privacy-preserving explanation
description: This flow delivers a test request form whose purpose is to enable collection of a biological specimen from the patient. A privacy threat exists if the patient is not clearly informed, at the point of handoff, what specimen will be collected, what personal and genetic information it may reveal, and who will receive it, undermining informed expectations around collection of highly sensitive data.
assumptions: Assumes the request form or clinician explanation may omit or inadequately communicate privacy-relevant details of downstream specimen collection and analysis.
uncertainty_note: Grounded in PA03.11 because this form directly initiates biological-sample collection, though the actual sample is collected in a subsequent step rather than on this flow itself.

title: Request form may expose sensitive health or testing context to unintended observers
description: The physical test request form can act as a record of the patient's condition, requested genetic test, or other identifying context. When handed to the patient, visible paper content may be seen, copied, or retained by others, disclosing sensitive medical or genetic-testing information beyond the intended recipient.
assumptions: Assumes the form contains patient identifiers and test-related information and is physically carried by the patient to another party.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 is used best-effort here because the form is a physical artifact/record associated with the patient; the strongest privacy issue is disclosure from the recorded content rather than the act of creating the record.

title: Sample-request handoff may create linkability between patient identity and future genetic specimen
description: By giving the patient a test request form that accompanies specimen collection, the flow can establish or preserve a linkage between the patient's identity and the biological sample later submitted to the sequencing lab. If the form includes identifiers, accession details, or barcodes, parties handling the sample can more easily correlate the specimen with the individual across collection and analysis stages.
assumptions: Assumes the form or attached labels contain identifiers or reference numbers reused during collection and laboratory intake.
uncertainty_note: This linkability risk is plausible for specimen workflows, but exact identifiers present on the form are not stated in the flow description.

title: Collection of biological specimen reveals sensitive health data
description: When the clinician retrieves and takes possession of the patient's physical sample, they are collecting a biological specimen from the data subject. Biological samples inherently contain highly sensitive health and genetic information, so this collection step creates a privacy threat of disclosure if more information can be derived from the specimen than the patient expects or is necessary for the stated care purpose.
assumptions: The sample is identifiable or reasonably linkable to the patient and is handled for diagnosis, treatment, or related clinical purposes.
uncertainty_note: The flow wording says the clinician retrieves a physical sample already referenced by a request, so this is slightly indirect versus initial sample taking; I still map it to PANOPTIC PA03.11 because custody transfer to the clinician constitutes collection/obtaining of a biological specimen.

title: Excessive collection through retrieval of a physical sample
description: Retrieving the full physical sample may collect more biological material and thus more personal information than is necessary for the immediate clinical task. Because biological specimens can support secondary testing or inference beyond the original request, this flow risks disproportionate data collection relative to purpose limitation and data minimization.
assumptions: Only part of the specimen or a less information-rich representation might have sufficed for the intended purpose.
uncertainty_note: This depends on whether the entire sample is actually needed; if retrieval is strictly necessary for the requested analysis, the disproportionate-collection concern is weaker.

title: Sample retrieval enables linkage of specimen to patient identity
description: The act of retrieving the patient's sample for the clinician implies the specimen is associated with identifiers or contextual metadata sufficient to connect the biological material to a specific patient. This creates a linkability threat because the sample and any resulting observations can be tied back to the individual across clinical records or other datasets.
assumptions: The specimen is labeled, tracked, or otherwise associated with patient identity or a stable pseudonym.

title: Collection of biological sample enables identification through specimen handling
description: Receiving the physical sample at the sequencing lab constitutes collection of biological material. Even before sequencing, custody and labeling of the specimen can directly identify or strongly link the sample to the patient, creating a detectability risk for the data subject.
assumptions: The sample is accompanied by labels, accession data, or other handling metadata sufficient to distinguish the subject or link the specimen to a person.

title: Biological specimen collection exposes highly sensitive personal data
description: A biological sample inherently contains rich sensitive information about the data subject, including genetic and health-related attributes. Receipt of the specimen by the sequencing lab creates a disclosure-of-information risk if the sample is accessed, mishandled, or repurposed beyond strictly controlled laboratory handling.
assumptions: The sample is human-derived and can reveal health or genetic characteristics if examined or retained.

title: Transfer and intake of the specimen create linkability between patient identity and future research data
description: By accepting the physical sample for sequencing, the receiving clerk enables linkage between the originating clinical context and the research outputs later derived from the specimen. Sample identifiers, chain-of-custody records, or accompanying paperwork may allow records across contexts to be correlated.
assumptions: The specimen is accompanied by persistent identifiers or paperwork that can be correlated with later sequencing outputs or other records.

title: Sample intake may exceed the permitted collection scope
description: Receipt of the physical sample may go beyond the scope authorized by consent, protocol, or governance rules if the sequencing lab collects or accepts specimens not covered by the stated research purpose, population, or retention conditions. This creates a non-compliance risk at the point of intake.
assumptions: Collection and transfer are subject to bounded consent, ethics approval, policy, or legal restrictions.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on external consent/protocol constraints that are not explicit in the flow description.

title: Re-identification risk from requested digital sample data
description: The request flow can enable retrieval of digital sample data that had been de-identified or pseudonymized, but remains linkable back to an individual when combined with other attributes, metadata, or external datasets available to the requester or downstream recipients. This creates a privacy threat at the Digital Sample Data Store when fulfilling the request.
assumptions: Assumes the digital sample data contains genomic or similarly distinctive sample-derived information, or rich metadata, that can support re-identification when disclosed for sequencing-lab use.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC PA05.01.01 is a strong semantic fit for genomic/sample-derived data, but the exact identifiability of the stored digital sample data is not explicitly stated in the flow description.

title: Excessive disclosure of recorded digital sample artifacts
description: The request may cause the store to disclose a digital artifact representing aspects of a data subject, such as recorded sample-derived data or associated files, beyond what is necessary for the sequencing purpose. Because these artifacts can reveal sensitive characteristics, releasing them from the store on request creates a disclosure risk.
assumptions: Assumes the 'digital sample data' includes recorded digital artifacts derived from a subject's specimen or testing process.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 'Recording' was retrieved and is plausibly relevant because the flow concerns digital sample data, but the exact PANOPTIC sub-activity governing downstream disclosure may be broader than collection/recording alone.

title: Lack of subject access or visibility into digital sample data sharing
description: If the store processes this request and releases digital sample data to support sequencing without enabling the data subject or their proxy to know what data was held and shared, the subject may be unable to access or inspect their information and its disclosure context. This undermines controllability and awareness over the sharing event.
assumptions: Assumes there is no separate mechanism informing data subjects about this request or allowing them to review the stored digital sample data released.
uncertainty_note: This is an indirect threat tied to the sharing flow rather than the request message itself; applicability depends on whether subject-access features exist elsewhere in the system.

title: Researcher access to digital sample artifacts may exceed data minimization expectations
description: When the NCCoE Researcher retrieves digital sample data from the Digital Sample Data Store, the flow transfers a digital artifact representing a subject or subject-linked sample. If the retrieved sample contains more detail than is necessary for the stated research task, the retrieval itself creates a privacy threat of unnecessary disclosure or exposure of personal data embedded in the artifact.
assumptions: Assumes the digital sample data can contain personal or subject-linked information and that researchers may retrieve full-resolution or full-content artifacts rather than a minimized view.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC retrieval activities were not provided in the supplied context; PA03.09 (Recording) is used as the closest match because the object being retrieved is a digital artifact, but the fit is approximate for a store-to-process access flow.

title: Retrieved digital sample data may enable implicit identification by the researcher
description: Digital sample data retrieved from the store may contain distinctive features or be linkable with request metadata and other research context, allowing the NCCoE Researcher to infer or confirm the identity of the data subject even if the sample is not explicitly labeled with direct identifiers.
assumptions: Assumes the digital sample data or associated request context contains quasi-identifiers, unique patterns, or linkable metadata.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on the actual richness and uniqueness of the digital sample data and whether the researcher has access to auxiliary data sources for linkage.

title: Researcher retrieval of digital sample data can support linkability across requests or datasets
description: By retrieving digital sample data referenced by a request, the researcher may be able to correlate the sample artifact with prior requests, related records, or external datasets. This can make multiple interactions or records concerning the same data subject linkable, even where direct identity is not initially known.
assumptions: Assumes stable identifiers, consistent sample characteristics, or reusable metadata are present across requests or repositories.
uncertainty_note: PA05.01 directly supports identification and often implies linkability in practice, but the exact PANOPTIC sub-activity for correlation/linking was not present in the supplied context.

title: Unnecessary receipt of biological sample by lab technician
description: The physical transfer of a biological sample to the lab technician exposes sensitive specimen material. If the technician receives the sample without a need strictly tied to the relevant research project, the flow enables disclosure of highly sensitive health/genetic information embodied in the specimen.
assumptions: Assumes the sample is identifiable or reasonably linkable to a data subject and that not every lab technician is authorized for every specimen.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort because PANOPTIC is primary here and the exact LINDDUN disclosure subtree for physical sample receipt is approximate.

title: Biological sample transfer out of approved collection/use scope
description: Sending the physical sample to the lab technician may exceed the scope under which the sample was originally collected or approved if the technician, project, or intended analysis is outside the permitted protocol, consent, or governance boundary. This creates a policy/compliance privacy threat at the point of receipt and use.
assumptions: Assumes sample use is bounded by consent, ethics approval, protocol, contract, or similar governance constraints.
uncertainty_note: PA06.09 is retrieved as collection out of scope; applying it to this transfer/use step is a best-effort interpretation that the receipt operationalizes an out-of-scope collection/use boundary violation.

title: Lab technician can link specimen to a specific subject or cohort
description: Receipt of the physical sample may allow the lab technician to link the specimen to an identifiable individual or a narrowly defined cohort, especially if labels, chain-of-custody details, or contextual project knowledge accompany the sample. The transfer therefore creates a linkability threat beyond what is necessary for the technician's task.
assumptions: Assumes the sample or accompanying handling context contains direct identifiers, coded identifiers, or distinctive attributes enabling linkage.
uncertainty_note: Linkability depends on whether the specimen is coded/de-identified before transfer; flow description alone does not confirm that detail.

title: Collection of biological specimen by the wet lab enables sensitive personal data acquisition
description: Receiving the physical sample at the wet lab constitutes collection/handling of a biological specimen for sequencing. Biological samples inherently contain extensive sensitive personal data (e.g., genetic information), creating a privacy threat if the sample is collected or further processed beyond the data subject's expectations or without adequate constraints.
assumptions: The wet lab's receipt of the sample is part of the specimen-collection/processing chain and the sample is linkable to an individual or case.
uncertainty_note: PA03.11 is a strong semantic fit even though the flow models transfer of an already-collected sample rather than the initial act of taking the specimen from the data subject.

title: Wet lab receipt of the sample may occur without sufficient awareness or consent for downstream genomic use
description: Transferring a physical sample to the wet lab can create a non-compliance risk if the data subject was not adequately informed that their specimen would be sequenced, retained, or used for specific downstream purposes. Because biological samples enable rich inference, insufficient notice, consent, or purpose limitation at this handoff is a privacy threat.
assumptions: Applicable where sequencing, retention, secondary use, or sharing terms are not fully covered by the original collection notice/consent.
uncertainty_note: Mapped to Dd as a policy/expectation mismatch around specimen use; exact LINDDUN tree-node granularity may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Biological sample sent for sequencing may permit identity linkage or re-identification
description: A physical biological sample delivered to the wet lab may be labeled directly or be indirectly linkable through case metadata. Even if pseudonymized, sequencing output or the specimen itself can often be re-associated with the data subject, enabling linkage across datasets or revealing that the individual participated in testing.
assumptions: The sample is accompanied by identifiers, quasi-identifiers, chain-of-custody information, or genomic data capable of re-identification.
uncertainty_note: PA05.01.01 is relevant when pseudonymization or de-identification is assumed; if the sample is directly identified, the threat is more straightforward linkage than re-identification.

title: Recording of genetic counseling session or results copy creates onward-disclosure risk
description: During the counselor-to-patient results review, the patient may receive a copy of the interpreted clinical results and may also record the consultation or retain screenshots/photos of the results. Those artifacts can later be shared with family members, employers, insurers, or other third parties beyond the originally intended context, increasing the risk of personal and especially sensitive genetic information being disseminated.
assumptions: The flow explicitly includes providing the patient a copy of the results; recording by the patient or others is plausible in in-person or virtual counseling contexts.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 is the closest retrieved PANOPTIC action because it concerns creation of a physical/digital artifact. The exact LINDDUN tree node is best-effort because PANOPTIC, not DFD position alone, is primary here.

title: Patient may be unable to independently manage the content or copies of delivered results
description: If the patient receives the interpreted results only in a fixed format or through a constrained channel, they may be unable to edit, redact, segment, or otherwise manage the information content before using it in other contexts. This can force over-disclosure of sensitive genetic findings when sharing results with another clinician, family member, school, employer, or insurer.
assumptions: The organization may provide the results as a static document or portal view with limited redaction/export controls.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on how the copy of results is delivered. If the patient can readily redact or selectively share content, PA07.02 may not apply.

title: Patient may lack control over onward disclosure of interpreted genetic results
description: When the Genetic Physician delivers interpreted clinical results and recommendations to the patient, the patient may have limited practical or procedural control over how those results are subsequently shared within the care setting or with other parties. If the disclosure occurs without granular consent options, clear sharing boundaries, or ability to defer/include certain result components, the patient can lose control over information disclosure for highly sensitive genetic information.
assumptions: Assumes the communication of results may be tied to broader clinical workflows or default sharing practices, rather than being fully under patient-directed disclosure control.
uncertainty_note: PA07.04 is a reasonable fit where result disclosure is not sufficiently controllable by the patient, but the flow text alone does not confirm whether granular consent or sharing controls are absent.

title: Interpreted genetic results could be intercepted in transit to the patient
description: The flow transmits sensitive interpreted clinical genetic results and professional recommendations from the physician to the patient. If communicated over insecure channels or in an environment where communications can be observed, an attacker or unintended recipient could intercept the information in transit, exposing highly sensitive health and genetic data.
assumptions: Assumes the communication traverses a channel susceptible to interception, such as insecure messaging, email, phone, postal handling, or in-person disclosure in insufficiently private settings.
uncertainty_note: The retrieved PANOPTIC activity PA03.07 clearly matches interception of a data flow, but the specific communication medium for GF17 is not provided, so applicability depends on implementation.

title: Clinical report generation uses research data beyond permitted scope
description: The Clinical Result Generation App receives context-relevant research data from the Cluster Filesystem to create a final clinical report. This creates a privacy threat if the transferred dataset includes attributes collected or retained for research purposes that are outside the scope, legal basis, or patient expectations for direct clinical reporting. The app may then incorporate out-of-scope data into a clinical artifact, causing inappropriate disclosure or use of data types beyond established limits.
assumptions: Assumes the research dataset can contain fields, annotations, or derived data not strictly necessary or authorized for clinical reporting, and that scope enforcement is not guaranteed before or during transfer.
uncertainty_note: PA06.08 is a strong fit if research and clinical-use boundaries differ, which is common; however, the flow description alone does not prove that out-of-scope attributes are actually present.

title: Lack of policy compliance checks when importing research data into clinical reporting
description: When the Clinical Result Generation App ingests research data from the Cluster Filesystem, it may fail to enforce purpose limitation, approved data categories, or governance constraints before using the data in a clinical report. This can result in non-compliant processing of personal data, especially where research data is reused in a distinct clinical context without adequate boundary checks.
assumptions: Assumes the application is responsible for validating whether incoming research data is permissible for clinical use and that such validation may be absent or incomplete.
uncertainty_note: Mapped to the compliance aspect of PA06.08 because the risk stems from use of data outside established limits; exact PANOPTIC fit is best-effort from available context.

title: Re-identification of patient across prior study records
description: The 3rd Party Previous Enrollment Entity receives results tied to a patient re-identification request and can re-associate previously de-identified or weakly linked study records with the identified patient, updating records across studies the patient is involved in.
assumptions: Assumes the prior enrollment entity maintains study records that are de-identified, pseudonymized, or otherwise separable from direct identity and that the transmitted results or accompanying identifiers enable re-linkage.
uncertainty_note: High confidence that re-identification is central to the described flow; tree node is best-effort because exact available LINDDUN Pro node set was not provided.

title: Oversharing to a third party during record update request
